chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
title: After-hours jam sessions; Frank Higgs makes him play I Got Rhythm in B-flat
summary: Big-band players jam at his beer garden job; a tenor player forces him to play in B-flat, and he learns tunes and chord calls from horn players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So there was all this music around, and I had to listen to it, and I was growing by leaps and bounds. And at this particular job where I was working, whenever these fellows got off from work... Then as now, whenever guys work in a big band, they never get enough of a chance to play, or never get to play long enough. So usually, when guys work in big bands,

if they like to play, they usually seek somewhere to play afterwards, which brought about jam sessions of all kinds. And at my place, where this drummer and I were working, these musicians used to come there after they got off of work. They would come in and they'd play until we got off of work.

I remember once... There was a tenor saxophone player then who later became a lawyer -- his name was Frank Higgs. He had learned a solo that was played by the tenor saxophone player with Andy Kirk. I'm trying to remember his name...

Yeah. Dick Wilson. Dick Wilson played a tenor saxophone solo on a thing called "Christopher Columbus." And Frank had just learned this solo, and so he came in that night and he asked me if I knew "I Got Rhythm." So I said, "Yeah." He said, "What key do you play it in." And I said I played it in C. He said, "I want you to play it in B-flat." I said, "I can't play it in B-flat." At that particular time, I could only play in C, F and G, and I think I had a couple of numbers I could play in E-flat, which was the thing that I had told this drummer before I took the job. But at that particular time, what did the drummer care about what key you played in. It didn't make any difference to him. He didn't know, I guess, that I was going to run into this situation. So finally, this fellow Frank Higgs said, "Can't you play

anything in B-flat?" -- because he wanted to show off this solo that he'd learned. I said, "Oh, no, I can't play anything." He said, "Do you know a B-flat chord?" I said, "Oh yeah." He said, "Well, play a B-flat chord and just keep playing the chord over and over." And he played this solo. When he got to the bridge, which went through a D-seven and a G-seven, a C-seven, F, he said "Just lay out there; don't play anything there." And after he finished the bridge, I came back and played some more B-flat.

So after that particular night, I hurried home, and the next day I was up early learning this particular tune in B-flat, which was a very easy transposition to make -- although I didn't know it at that particular time. And that next night I went back, I was ready for him!

It was things like that that really made me learn. Just picking up something here and there from different musicians, hearing a hint here... A lot of horn players used to come around who actually knew chords themselves, and I knew my chords pretty well, and they would play their horn, and after each phrase take their horn out their mouths and call the chord to me, and I would play it. A lot of things I learned like that. Whatever happened, if I ran across something that stumped me, I'd always go back and get some music.
